ADY201m — Cardiovascular disease: analysis and classification¶

Data: data/cardio_train_raw.csv — 70,000 patients, 13 columns (11 input features, ID, target CARDIO), semicolon-separated, AGE in days. This notebook reads the raw file and converts age exactly once, so it does not depend on the export from notebook 01 and cannot convert age twice.

Contents

  1. Setup, data and quality checks
  2. Exploratory analysis and visualisation
  3. Blood-pressure cleaning with the IQR rule (for EDA and statistics)
  4. Statistical tests and OLS (as required by the brief)
  5. Modelling: leakage-free pipelines, model comparison, hyper-parameter tuning
  6. Evaluation of the selected model
  7. Conclusions and limitations

All figures are written to figures/ and all tables, the trained model and predictions to results/.

def corr_heatmap(frame, title, name):
    corr = frame[FEATURES + [TARGET]].corr()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 8))
    sns.heatmap(corr, cmap=DIVERGING, vmin=-1, vmax=1, center=0, annot=True, fmt=".2f",

    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(False)
    save(fig, name)
    return corr[TARGET].drop(TARGET).sort_values(ascending=False)

3. Blood-pressure cleaning with the IQR rule¶

For AP_HI and AP_LO: IQR = Q3 − Q1, lower limit = Q1 − 1.5·IQR, upper limit = Q3 + 1.5·IQR. Values outside the limits are capped to the nearest limit (rows are kept).

These full-data limits are used only for EDA and the statistical tests. In section 5 the same rule lives inside each model pipeline and is learned from the training data alone.

In [8]:
clean = df.copy()
rows = []
for col in BLOOD_PRESSURE:
    low, high = iqr_limits(df[col])
    rows.append({"column": col, "lower": low, "upper": high,
                 "capped_below": int((df[col] < low).sum()), "capped_above": int((df[col] > high).sum())})
    clean[col] = df[col].clip(low, high)
limits = pd.DataFrame(rows)
limits.to_csv(RES / "iqr_limits.csv", index=False)
clean.to_csv(DATA / "cardio_train_clean.csv", index=False)

4. Statistical tests (α = 0.05)¶

Reject H₀ when p < 0.05. With 70,000 rows almost any difference is "significant", so each test also reports an effect size to show how large the difference is.

In [11]:
tests = []


def record(name, h0, statistic, p, effect, measure):
    tests.append({"test": name, "H0": h0, "statistic": statistic, "p_value": p,
                  "effect_size": effect, "effect_measure": measure,
                  "decision": "reject H0" if p < 0.05 else "fail to reject H0"})


groups = [clean.loc[clean.CHOLESTEROL == k, TARGET] for k in (1, 2, 3)]
f, p = stats.f_oneway(*groups)
grand = clean[TARGET].mean()
eta2 = sum(len(g) * (g.mean() - grand) ** 2 for g in groups) / ((clean[TARGET] - grand) ** 2).sum()
record("One-way ANOVA: CHOLESTEROL vs CARDIO", "CHOLESTEROL is not related to the disease", f, p, eta2, "eta squared")

younger = clean.loc[clean.AGE < clean.AGE.mean(), TARGET]
older = clean.loc[clean.AGE >= clean.AGE.mean(), TARGET]
lev, lev_p = stats.levene(younger, older, center="mean")
record("Levene: equal variances of CARDIO, younger vs older", "variances are equal", lev, lev_p, np.nan, "")
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(younger, older, equal_var=lev_p > 0.05)
record("Welch t-test: AGE (split at mean) vs CARDIO", "AGE is not related to the disease", t, p,
       older.mean() - younger.mean(), "difference in disease rate (older - younger)")

r, p = stats.pearsonr(clean.WEIGHT, clean[TARGET])
record("Pearson (point-biserial): WEIGHT vs CARDIO", "WEIGHT is not related to the disease", r, p, r, "correlation r")

for col in ["ALCO", "SMOKE", "ACTIVE"]:
    table = pd.crosstab(clean[col], clean[TARGET])
    chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=True)
    cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (table.values.sum() * (min(table.shape) - 1)))
    record(f"Chi-square: {col} vs CARDIO", f"{col} is not related to the disease", chi2, p, cramers_v, "Cramer's V")

tests = pd.DataFrame(tests)
tests.to_csv(RES / "statistical_tests.csv", index=False)
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 60)
tests.style.format({"statistic": "{:.3f}", "p_value": "{:.3g}", "effect_size": "{:.4f}"})

Interpretation

Hypothesis Result Effect size
CHOLESTEROL not related ANOVA F ≈ 1800, p ≈ 0 → reject H₀ η² ≈ 0.049 (small–medium): disease rate rises from 44 % to 77 % across levels
AGE not related Levene p < 0.05, so Welch's t-test; t ≈ −52.5, p ≈ 0 → reject H₀ older half: +19.6 percentage points disease rate
WEIGHT not related Pearson r ≈ 0.18, p ≈ 0 → reject H₀ weak positive correlation
ALCO not related χ² ≈ 3.70, p ≈ 0.055 → fail to reject H₀ Cramér's V ≈ 0.007 (negligible)
SMOKE not related χ² ≈ 16.7, p < 0.001 → reject H₀ V ≈ 0.015 (negligible)
ACTIVE not related χ² ≈ 88.8, p < 0.001 → reject H₀ V ≈ 0.036 (very small); active patients 49 % vs 54 %

SMOKE is "significant" only because n is huge: the effect is negligible, and smokers actually show a lower rate (47.5 % vs 50.2 %). Smoking is self-reported and concentrated among men, so this is a confounded association, not a protective effect.

OLS model¶

A linear probability model on all 11 features (cleaned blood pressure) shows each feature's association with CARDIO while holding the others fixed. It reproduces the brief's statsmodels step; the classifiers in section 5 handle the binary target properly.

Interpretation: R² = 0.235. Holding the other features fixed, AP_HI (t ≈ 64), AGE (t ≈ 40), CHOLESTEROL (t ≈ 34), WEIGHT and AP_LO have positive, significant coefficients; ACTIVE is negative (exercise is associated with lower risk). GENDER is not significant (p ≈ 0.33). GLUC, SMOKE and ALCO turn slightly negative once correlated factors (cholesterol, gender) are controlled for — a sign of confounding and self-reporting in this dataset, so these coefficients should not be read causally. The large condition number reflects unscaled features, not a modelling error.

5. Modelling¶

Split: 70 % train (49,000) / 30 % test (21,000), stratified on CARDIO, random_state = 42. Train/test IDs are saved to results/.

Leakage-free pipeline: every model is wrapped as IQRClipper → StandardScaler (numeric columns) → classifier. Both preprocessing steps learn their parameters inside fit, i.e. only from the training data — and only from the training folds during cross-validation.

Selection rule: the model is chosen by 3-fold cross-validated accuracy on the training set. The test set is used once, to report the chosen model's performance; the test scores of the other models are shown for comparison only.

In [14]:
X, y = df[FEATURES], df[TARGET]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
pd.DataFrame({"ID": df.loc[X_train.index, "ID"]}).to_csv(RES / "train_ids.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame({"ID": df.loc[X_test.index, "ID"]}).to_csv(RES / "test_ids.csv", index=False)
print(f"Train: {X_train.shape}  disease rate {y_train.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Test:  {X_test.shape}  disease rate {y_test.mean():.3f}")


def make_pipeline(model):
    scale = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), NUMERIC)], remainder="passthrough",
                              verbose_feature_names_out=False)
    return Pipeline([("iqr", IQRClipper()), ("scale", scale), ("model", model)])


cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)

Train: (49000, 11)  disease rate 0.500
Test:  (21000, 11)  disease rate 0.500

Hyper-parameter tuning of Gradient Boosting¶

8 combinations × 3 folds on the training set.

In [15]:
grid = GridSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED)),
    {"model__n_estimators": [100, 200], "model__learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1], "model__max_depth": [3, 4]},
    cv=cv, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=-1,
)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

Model comparison¶

Each model: 3-fold CV accuracy on the training set, then one fit on the full training set and scores on the test set. A majority-class DummyClassifier is the floor every model must beat.

In [16]:
candidates = {
    "Dummy baseline": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "RidgeClassifier": RidgeClassifier(alpha=1e-4),
    "RandomForest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
    "ExtraTrees": ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
    "AdaBoost": AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=SEED),
    "Bagging KNN": BaggingClassifier(KNeighborsClassifier(), max_samples=0.5, max_features=0.5,
                                     random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
    "GradientBoosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED),
    "Stacking": StackingClassifier(
        estimators=[("ridge", RidgeClassifier()), ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=20))],
        final_estimator=GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=25, subsample=0.5, min_samples_leaf=25,
                                                   max_features=1, random_state=SEED),
        n_jobs=-1),
}


def scores(pipe):
    pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
    if hasattr(pipe, "predict_proba"):
        score = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    else:
        score = pipe.decision_function(X_test)
    return pred, score, {
        "test_accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, pred),
        "precision": precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(y_test, pred),
        "f1": f1_score(y_test, pred),
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_test, score),
    }


fitted, predictions, rows = {}, {}, []
for name, model in candidates.items():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pipe = make_pipeline(model)
    cv_acc = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=-1).mean()
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
    pred, score, metrics = scores(pipe)
    fitted[name], predictions[name] = pipe, (pred, score)
    rows.append({"model": name, "cv_accuracy": cv_acc, **metrics, "seconds": time.perf_counter() - start})
    print(f"{name:<22} CV {cv_acc:.4f}   test {metrics['test_accuracy']:.4f}")

tuned = grid.best_estimator_
pred, score, metrics = scores(tuned)
fitted["GradientBoosting tuned"], predictions["GradientBoosting tuned"] = tuned, (pred, score)
rows.append({"model": "GradientBoosting tuned", "cv_accuracy": grid.best_score_, **metrics, "seconds": np.nan})

comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("cv_accuracy", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
comparison.to_csv(RES / "model_comparison.csv", index=False)
selected = comparison.loc[0, "model"]
print("\nSelected by CV accuracy:", selected)
comparison.round(4)

Figure 9 — Feature importance¶

Permutation importance on the test set: how much accuracy drops when one feature is shuffled. It is model-agnostic and measured on unseen data.

7. Conclusions and limitations¶

Findings

  • Data quality: no missing values or duplicate IDs, but the blood-pressure columns contain 1,000+ impossible readings. Capping them with the IQR rule turns AP_HI from an apparently weak feature into the strongest one.
  • Risk factors: systolic blood pressure, cholesterol and age are the main factors — confirmed by the correlation after cleaning, the statistical tests, the OLS model and the permutation importance of the final model. Weight matters to a lesser degree; physical activity is mildly protective; alcohol shows no significant effect.
  • Classification: all models beat the 50 % baseline by a wide margin. Selected by cross-validation, the tuned Gradient Boosting (learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 4, n_estimators = 200) reaches 73.4 % accuracy, 0.80 ROC-AUC, 0.75 precision and 0.70 recall on the untouched test set. CV and test accuracy differ by less than 0.3 points, so the estimate is stable. Random Forest and Extra Trees over-fit the noisy features and score lowest.

Limitations

  • Tests show statistical association on observational data, not causation; with 70,000 rows, p-values must be read together with effect sizes.
  • SMOKE, ALCO and ACTIVE are self-reported, and some rows remain implausible after capping (e.g. heights below 120 cm), which caps achievable accuracy around 73–74 %.
  • Missing a sick patient is costlier than a false alarm; in practice the decision threshold should be lowered to raise recall (0.70 now) at the expense of precision.
  • The model is for coursework only and has not been validated for clinical use.
